title: The best research finds the fact that changes the argument.
dek: In Chapter 11, Claude C. Hopkins makes research part of the craft itself. The advertiser's job is to keep looking until one exact fact gives the reader a reason to believe and act.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: Research is not a ceremony before the real work. It is how the real work discovers what the product can honestly and memorably say.

canon.heading: Hopkins: the useful fact is usually hiding behind the obvious one.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 11, "Information," from Claude C. Hopkins's Scientific Advertising, on PDF pages 34-36. Hopkins argues that the advertiser earns the right to make a claim by doing the patient work that uncovers the fact behind it.
canon.readerIntro: Read for Hopkins's examples of research changing the appeal itself. Mark the point where information becomes a selling idea, where consumer and competitor evidence enters the work, and where an exact fact makes an impressive claim more believable.

blocks.label: 01 / The fact is the raw material
paragraphs: Hopkins treats information as the beginning of intelligent advertising. Before writing, the advertiser has to know the product, the category, the customer, and the competing claims well enough to find what is genuinely useful.
The point is not to collect facts for their own sake. It is to find the fact that changes what the reader can understand or believe.

blocks.label: 02 / Research can change the appeal
paragraphs: The chapter's strongest examples show research overturning the obvious sales story. A market may appear to want one thing while the evidence reveals a different tension or a more powerful reason to choose.
That is why surface familiarity is dangerous. The first plausible claim is often the least distinctive one.

blocks.label: 03 / Exactness turns assertion into evidence
paragraphs: A general statement can sound impressive and still leave no picture in the reader's mind. Hopkins shows how measurement, testing, and technical verification give the claim edges that make it easier to trust.
Specificity is not decoration added after the idea. It is the proof that lets the idea carry weight.

blocks.label: 04 / Consumer knowledge prevents expensive guessing
paragraphs: Hopkins describes interviews, questionnaires, home visits, competitor research, and long reading because the advertiser needs to understand the actual buying situation rather than imagine it from an office.
The research may look disproportionate to the final ad. That is the point: simplicity in the finished message can be the visible result of complexity backstage.

blocks.label: 05 / The apprentice test
paragraphs: Take one claim you want to make and ask what evidence would make it more exact, more surprising, or more useful. Then go looking for that evidence before polishing the sentence.
The work is finished when the research has found a fact the market can recognize and the product can honestly own.

What important claim in your own work still rests on office intuition rather than evidence?

principle.heading: Research until the product gives you a sharper truth.
principle.body: Hopkins's lesson is that better copy often begins as better observation. The advertiser who knows the category, the customer, the rivals, and the measurable product facts can make a claim that feels discovered rather than manufactured.
principle.example: Instead of saying a meal-delivery service is convenient, interview customers about the exact evening problem it removes. The strongest claim may be the recurring moment at 8:40 pm when a parent avoids another trip to the shop.
principle.practice: Choose one important claim. List the five facts that would make it more credible or distinctive, then find one through a customer conversation, product test, competitor review, or direct observation.

signals.heading: Four fresh signals on product theatre, category framing, recurring rituals, and evidence-led brand work.

fieldNotes.title: Apple's foldable iPhone turns a long rumor into a product category test
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Apple's September event introduced the foldable iPhone Duo alongside the iPhone 18 Pro, AirPods 5, and new Apple Watch models.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A product that has existed as rumor now has to earn a daily use case. The launch challenge shifts from making the form surprising to proving why the fold changes the user's life.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether Apple can turn the fold into a repeated behavior rather than a launch spectacle, especially at a premium price.

fieldNotes.title: Autodesk puts makers and customers at the centre of its technology story
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Autodesk launched The World Is Yours for the Making, a global brand campaign centred on the architects, engineers, builders, designers, manufacturers, filmmakers, and creators who use its tools.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The campaign makes the user's finished work the evidence of the software's value. It sells capability through visible human outcomes rather than through a list of technical features.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the customer stories create a sharper mental category for Autodesk than generic claims about creative technology.

fieldNotes.title: VIRGIO turns a weekly fashion drop into a recurring ritual
fieldNotes.whatHappened: VIRGIO expanded its VIRGIO MOD Thursday campaign with a new film, using a consistent weekly drop cadence to give shoppers a recurring reason to return.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The brand is not treating every launch as a one-off announcement. It is attaching newness to a memorable time cue, making the shopping habit part of the product experience.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the Thursday ritual creates repeat behaviour and memory, or simply adds another promotional date to the calendar.

fieldNotes.title: Vodafone uses action-movie language to make network performance felt
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Vodafone launched SuperMobile with Leo UK, using Roman Kemp and action-movie tropes to dramatise faster speeds and guaranteed minimum speeds across TV, digital, video, social, and out-of-home.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Network performance is difficult to see in an ad. The campaign translates a technical advantage into an emotional state, giving the claim a scene the audience can inhabit.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the theatrical metaphor remains connected to the measurable speed promise across the full campaign system.

output.heading: Find the fact behind the claim.
output.body: Choose one claim you want to make. Identify the evidence that would make it sharper, then go find one fact before you rewrite the sentence.
